questions.question: 100 coroutines on `Dispatchers.Default` each increment a plain `var` 1000 times. What gets printed?
options: Usually less than 100000, and it varies between runs
Always exactly 100000
Always exactly 1000
It doesn't compile: a top-level `var` can't be changed from a coroutine
questions.explanation: `count++` is a read, an add and a write. Coroutines on different `Default` threads interleave those steps and overwrite each other's updates, so increments get lost. Structured concurrency only guarantees all coroutines finish before the `println`, not that their updates are atomic.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: 10 20 30 done
done
10 done
questions.explanation: The `for` loop receives each element and ends when the channel is closed and empty, so `done` is printed. Without `ch.close()`, the loop would wait forever and the program would hang.

questions.question: `Channel<Int>()` with no arguments creates a rendezvous channel: `send` suspends until some receiver takes the element.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The default capacity is `Channel.RENDEZVOUS` (0). It has no buffer, so sender and receiver must meet. Use `Channel.BUFFERED`, `UNLIMITED` or a number to get a buffer.

questions.question: Many coroutines on `Dispatchers.Default` run `count++`. Which changes make the final count correct? Select all that apply.
options: Wrap the increment in `mutex.withLock { count++ }` using one shared `Mutex`
Make `count` an `AtomicInteger` and call `incrementAndGet()`
Run every increment on `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)`
Annotate `count` with `@Volatile`
Wrap `count++` in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`
questions.explanation: A mutex, an atomic read-modify-write, and confining the state to one-at-a-time execution all stop lost updates. `@Volatile` only makes writes visible to other threads. It doesn't make `++` atomic. `Dispatchers.IO` is multi-threaded too, so it fixes nothing.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: true true false false
true true true true
false false false false
true true true false
questions.explanation: A capacity of 2 buffers two elements. `trySend` never suspends: when the buffer is full and nobody is receiving, it returns a failed result instead of waiting, so the 3rd and 4th calls fail.

questions.question: A repository calls `save()` from a ViewModel. What happens?
options: `save()` suspends forever, because `log()` waits for a lock its caller holds
It works: the same coroutine can re-enter a lock it already holds
`log()` throws `IllegalStateException` straight away, because the lock is already taken
The second `withLock` is skipped because the lock is already held
questions.explanation: `kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex` is not reentrant. The coroutine already holds the lock in `save()`, so `log()` suspends waiting for it to be released, and that never happens: a deadlock. Unlike `synchronized`, a Mutex has no owner thread to recognise. Make the inner function lock-free or take the lock once at the outer level.

questions.question: What does `val numbers = produce { repeat(3) { send(it) } }` give you inside a `CoroutineScope`?
options: A `ReceiveChannel<Int>` that closes when the block finishes
A `SendChannel<Int>` that you must close yourself
A cold `Flow<Int>` that runs again for each collector
A `Job` whose result holds the three values
questions.explanation: `produce` launches a coroutine with a channel and returns its receiving side. When the block completes, the channel is closed (or closed with the exception if it fails), so consumers using `for (x in numbers)` end cleanly. It is hot, not a cold Flow.

questions.question: Everything runs on the single `runBlocking` thread. What does this print?
options:
send 0
sent 0
send 1
recv 0
recv 1
sent 1

send 0
recv 0
sent 0
send 1
recv 1
sent 1

send 0
sent 0
send 1
sent 1
recv 0
recv 1

send 0
recv 0
send 1
recv 1
sent 0
sent 1
questions.explanation: The receiver is already waiting, so `send(0)` hands the value over without suspending. The receiver is only scheduled to resume, so the producer prints `sent 0`, and `send(1)` then suspends because nobody is waiting. The receiver prints `recv 0`, takes 1 from the waiting sender without suspending, and prints `recv 1` before the producer gets to `sent 1`.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: the `delay` suspension point is inside a critical section
It compiles and holds the monitor while the coroutine is suspended
It compiles, but throws `IllegalMonitorStateException` when the coroutine resumes
It compiles, and `synchronized` releases the monitor automatically during `delay`
questions.explanation: A JVM monitor belongs to a thread, but a suspended coroutine may resume on a different thread, which could never release it. The compiler rejects suspension points inside `synchronized`. Use `Mutex.withLock` when the critical section has to suspend.

questions.question: When three worker coroutines all receive from the same channel (fan-out), every element is delivered to all three workers.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A channel element is consumed by exactly one receiver, so fan-out spreads the work between the workers. If every subscriber should see every value, use a `SharedFlow` instead.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: 4 end
0 end
It hangs on the second `send`
questions.explanation: A `CONFLATED` channel keeps only the latest element, and `send` never suspends: each new value replaces the one that hasn't been received yet. Only `4` is left when the loop starts receiving.

questions.question: A download manager keeps `completed` and `bytesDone` that must always be updated together, from many coroutines. Why is one `AtomicInteger` per field not enough?
options: Another coroutine can read between the two updates and see them out of step
`AtomicInteger` doesn't work from coroutines because they can switch threads
`AtomicInteger` increments are lost when the coroutine is cancelled
Two atomics on one object cause a deadlock
questions.explanation: Atomics protect a single variable. An invariant that covers several variables needs one critical section around both updates, for example `mutex.withLock { completed++; bytesDone += n }`. Atomics work fine from coroutines on any thread.

questions.question: A producer calls `channel.close()` while two elements are still in the buffer. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The two buffered elements are still delivered to receivers
A later `send` throws `ClosedSendChannelException`
`for (x in channel)` ends after the buffered elements are received
`close()` throws away the buffered elements immediately
`receive()` on the closed, empty channel returns `null`
questions.explanation: `close()` is a 'no more elements' signal: what is already buffered is still received, and then iteration ends. Discarding buffered elements is what `cancel()` does. `receive()` on a closed, empty channel throws `ClosedReceiveChannelException`. Use `receiveCatching()` for a non-throwing result.

questions.question: What does this print?
options:
7
null
closed

null
null
closed

7
7
closed

7
null
null
questions.explanation: Closing keeps the buffered `7`, so the first `receiveCatching()` succeeds. The second one finds the channel closed and empty and returns a closed `ChannelResult`, whose `getOrNull()` is `null`. Plain `receive()` throws `ClosedReceiveChannelException` instead.

questions.question: Inside a non-suspending `View.OnClickListener` you want to put a `ClickEvent` into a `Channel(Channel.BUFFERED)`. Which call fits?
options: `events.trySend(ClickEvent)`
`events.send(ClickEvent)`
`runBlocking { events.send(ClickEvent) }`
`events.close(ClickEvent)`
questions.explanation: `trySend` is the non-suspending version: it adds the element if there is room and returns a `ChannelResult` saying whether it worked. `send` is a suspend function and won't compile in a plain listener, and `runBlocking` would block the main thread.

questions.question: With `Channel<Int>(2, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)`, `send` never suspends: when the buffer is full, the oldest buffered element is dropped to make room.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With `DROP_OLDEST` or `DROP_LATEST`, a full buffer drops an element instead of making the sender wait. Only the default `BufferOverflow.SUSPEND` makes `send` suspend. `CONFLATED` is the same idea with a buffer of 1.

questions.question: Why do the coroutines docs use `for (x in channel)` rather than `channel.consumeEach { }` for fan-out workers that share one channel?
options: `consumeEach` cancels the channel when it exits, which stops the other workers too
`consumeEach` gives every element to every worker
`consumeEach` can only be called from `Dispatchers.Main`
`for (x in channel)` receives elements in batches, so each worker makes fewer suspending calls
questions.explanation: `consumeEach` assumes it is the only consumer: when it exits, normally or with an exception, it cancels the channel. That's handy for a single consumer but wrong when several workers share the channel. A `for` loop only stops the worker that is running it.

questions.question: All 100 coroutines run on the single `runBlocking` thread. What does this print?
questions.explanation: Confining state to one thread makes each step atomic, but not a read-then-write that suspends in between. All 100 coroutines read `0` before any of them resumes from `delay`, so each one writes `1`. Keep the read and the write in the same non-suspending step, or hold a `Mutex` across the whole sequence.

questions.question: A ViewModel sends navigation events. Why is `Channel(Channel.BUFFERED)` exposed with `receiveAsFlow()` often chosen over `MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>()` here?
options: Events sent while nothing is collecting wait in the buffer instead of being dropped
Every collector receives every event, so two screens observing the ViewModel can both react to it
A channel replays the last event to new collectors, like `StateFlow`
Channels are cold, so the event is only created when the UI collects
questions.explanation: `MutableSharedFlow()` with no replay drops emissions when there are no subscribers, so a navigation event sent during a configuration change can be lost. A buffered channel holds it until the new collector arrives. The trade-off is that each event goes to only one collector.

questions.question: Which statements correctly contrast channels with cold flows? Select all that apply.
options: A `produce` coroutine starts running as soon as it's launched, whether or not anyone receives yet
A `flow { }` block runs again from the start for each collector
A channel signals 'no more elements' with `close()`, while a flow completes when its block returns
A new receiver of a channel first gets the most recent element again, like `StateFlow`
A cold flow can be collected only once
questions.explanation: Channels are hot communication primitives: the producer runs on its own, and completion is signalled by closing. A cold flow does nothing until it is collected and restarts for every collector, so it can be collected many times. Channels don't replay anything: each element is received once.
